{{notability|date=March 2011}}

In [[computer science]], a '''predictive state representation''' ('''PSR''') is a way to model a state of controlled [[dynamical system]] from a history of actions taken and resulting observations. PSR captures the state of a system as a vector of predictions for future tests (experiments) that can be done on the system.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1145/1015330.1015359 |citeseerx=10.1.1.67.5179 |chapter=Learning and discovery of predictive state representations in dynamical systems with reset |title=Twenty-first international conference on Machine learning - ICML '04 |year=2004 |last1=James |first1=Michael R. |last2=Singh |first2=Satinder |page=53 |isbn=978-1-58113-838-2 |s2cid=9111832 }}</ref> A test is a sequence of action-observation pairs and its prediction is the probability of the test's observation-sequence happening if the test's action-sequence were to be executed on the system. One of the advantage of using PSR is that the predictions are directly related to observable quantities.  This is in contrast to other models of dynamical systems, such as [[partially observable Markov decision process]]es (POMDPs) where the state of the system is represented as a [[probability distribution]] over unobserved nominal states.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Izadi |first1=Masoumeh T. |last2=Precup |first2=Doina |title=A planning algorithm for predictive state representations |journal=Proceedings of the 18th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence |series=Ijcai'03 |date=9 August 2003 |pages=1520–1521 |url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.5555/1630659.1630919 }}</ref>

== Definition ==
Consider a dynamic system based on a discrete set <math>\mathcal A</math> of actions and a discrete set <math>\mathcal O</math> of observations.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Littman |first=Michael |last2=Sutton |first2=Richard S |date=2001 |title=Predictive Representations of State |url=https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2001/hash/1e4d36177d71bbb3558e43af9577d70e-Abstract.html |journal=Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems |publisher=MIT Press |volume=14}}</ref> A history <math>h</math> is a sequence <math>a_1 o_1 \dots a_\ell o_\ell</math> where <math>a_1 , \dots, a_\ell</math> are the actions taken by the agent in that order and <math>o_1 , \dots, o_\ell</math> are the observations made up by the agent. Let us write <math>P(a_1 o_1 \dots a_\ell o_\ell)</math> to be the conditional probability of observing <math>o_1 , \dots, o_\ell</math> given that the actions taken are <math>a_1 , \dots, a_\ell</math>.

We now want to characterize a given hidden state reached after some history <math>h</math>. To do that, we introduce the notion of test. A test <math>t</math> is of the same type that a history: it is a sequence of action-observation pairs. The idea is now to consider a set of tests <math>\{t_1, \dots, t_n\}</math> to full characterize a hidden state. To do that, we first define the probability of a test <math>t</math> conditional on a history <math>h</math>: <math>P(t \mid h) := \frac{P(ht)}{P(h)}</math>.

We now define the prediction vector <math>p(h) = [P(t_1\mid h), \dots, P(t_n\mid h)]</math>. We say that <math>p(h)</math> is a predictive state representation (PSR) if and only if it forms a sufficient statistic for the system. In other words,  <math>p(h)</math> is a predictive state representation (PSR) if and only if for all possible tests <math>t</math>, there exists a function <math>f_t</math> such that for all histories <math>h</math>, <math>P(t\mid h) = f_t(p(h))</math>.

The functions <math>f_t</math> are called ''projection functions''. We say that the PSR is linear when the function <math>f_t</math> is linear for all possible tests <math>t</math>. The main theorem proved in <ref name=":0" /> is stated as follows.

'''Theorem.''' Consider a finite POMDP with <math>k</math> states. Then there exists a linear PSR with a number of tests <math>n</math> smaller that <math>k</math>.
